title: GameDevBench: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Through Game Development
one_liner: Use game development as a hard benchmark for multimodal agents and show that direct image and video feedback can materially improve how those agents work.
lead: Game development is a demanding testbed for agents because the work combines code edits with visual assets, scene layout, animation, and real-time behavior. An agent must read files, understand how assets appear on screen, and decide whether the visible result matches the task. This paper turns that setting into a benchmark. It also shows that simple visual feedback, taken from rendered images or short videos, can help agents solve more of these tasks because text logs alone often miss what is visibly wrong.

problem.h2: Why ordinary coding benchmarks are not enough
paras: A normal coding benchmark can often be solved from text alone. The agent reads code, edits files, runs tests, and checks console output. Game development is harder because many important errors are visual: a sprite is misaligned, an animation timing is off, a shader produces the wrong color, or a scene behaves incorrectly even though the build succeeds.

Without a benchmark that mixes code and visible output, it is hard to measure how well an agent actually handles multimodal software work. It is also hard to test whether visual feedback mechanisms help, because the benchmark itself does not demand visual understanding in the first place.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Create a benchmark of real game-development tasks and evaluate whether agents improve when they can inspect rendered images or short videos from the game scene because those views reveal visible errors that logs do not show.

panels.title: 1. The task spans code and art assets
panels.viz_args: Scripts, sprites, shader files, scene output
panels.caption: Game tasks require both software changes and visual understanding.

panels.title: 2. Text-only checking misses visible bugs
panels.viz_args: Build passes, but the scene still looks wrong
panels.caption: Console success does not guarantee a correct visual result.

panels.title: 3. Benchmark many game tasks
panels.caption: The benchmark covers the kinds of multimodal tasks that ordinary software suites under-sample.

panels.title: 4. Add image or video feedback
panels.viz_args: Rendered frame or short clip returned to the agent
panels.caption: Visual feedback exposes errors that text logs do not report.

panels.title: 5. Measure true multimodal performance
panels.caption: Agents improve when they can see what the game scene actually does.

steps.text: Derive tasks from web and video tutorials so that they reflect realistic developer workflows.
Include code, assets, and scene behavior so that success depends on more than plain text editing.
Measure how many tasks current agents can solve without extra visual support.
Return rendered screenshots or short videos to the agent during problem solving.
Check which categories benefit most from visual feedback and where agents still struggle.

paras: The paper changes the evaluation target for software agents. Instead of measuring mostly text-centric development tasks, it measures work where the visible state of the program is part of the answer.
object.object: The benchmark used to measure multimodal software-agent capability

hidden.name: How far the visible result is from the intended game state
paras: The hidden quantity is the gap between the current rendered game state and the state the task actually asks for. Many code changes look reasonable in text form but still produce the wrong visual result. A text-only agent can miss that gap because it does not see the screen outcome directly.

The benchmark exposes this quantity by making visible correctness central to task completion. Image or video feedback then gives the agent direct evidence about that gap so that it can revise the code or assets based on what the player would actually see.

heat.caption: High values mark information sources that directly reveal whether the visible scene matches the intended task outcome.

reads.html: The hard part is not only editing code. It is seeing whether the on-screen result matches the requested game behavior.
GameDevBench measures multimodal agent skill by tying task success to rendered scene correctness and then testing whether simple visual feedback reduces that visible-task mismatch.

mechanism.h2: Why game development is a strong testbed
paras: Game tasks stress multimodal reasoning because code and assets interact tightly. A small logic change can affect movement, drawing order, shading, or animation timing. That means an agent must connect file edits to visible behavior rather than stopping after a successful build.

Visual feedback helps because it turns hidden scene errors into direct evidence. A screenshot can show a mispositioned object, and a short clip can reveal timing or motion issues. Those signals improve performance by giving the agent a tighter loop between edit and visible consequence.

stages.s: Game project with code, assets, and target task
Agent edits files and runs the project
Feed visual result back to the agent
Revise code and assets using visible evidence
Higher success on multimodal development tasks

math.words: Treat task success as a combination of code correctness and rendered-scene correctness, then compare performance with and without visual feedback.
math.equation: task_score = alpha * code_correctness + beta * visual_correctness ; feedback_gain = score_with_visual - score_text_only
symbols: overall score on one game-development task
whether the code and asset changes satisfy textual requirements
whether the rendered scene matches the intended visible result
improvement from adding image or video feedback

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Text-only agent fixes the build but leaves the sprite offset wrong: code_correctness = 0.9, visual_correctness = 0.3.
Agent with screenshot feedback notices the offset and fixes it: code_correctness = 0.9, visual_correctness = 0.85.
The gain comes from better visible correctness, not from better syntax alone.

math.note: The benchmark reports solved tasks rather than this exact score, but the score summarizes the central point: multimodal development success depends heavily on visible correctness.

charts.title: Text-only agent
charts.note: Agents perform much worse on visually demanding tasks because logs and code alone do not reveal enough about the rendered result.

charts.title: Agent with visual feedback
charts.note: Image and video feedback improve outcomes because the agent can detect visible errors and revise the project accordingly.

items.html: A single frame may hide animation or control problems, so video feedback is needed when timing matters.

items.b: Benchmark tasks can still be narrow.
items.html: If the tasks cluster around one engine or art style, the measured gains may not transfer cleanly to other game-development settings.
Poor camera placement or low-resolution captures can mislead the agent because the visible evidence does not clearly show the bug.
Use a diverse task set, pair screenshots with short clips when motion matters, and capture the scene from informative viewpoints so that visual feedback reflects the true task state.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark with several game tasks: move a sprite to the right position, fix a shader color, adjust animation timing, and repair a collision bug. For each task, compare an agent that sees only code and logs against one that also receives a rendered frame or short clip after each attempt. Measure solved tasks and break results down by task type.

The demo should prove that visual feedback matters most on tasks where the visible result carries essential information, because the agent can only correct those errors once it sees the screen state directly.
demo.closing: A strong demo shows that game development is a useful benchmark for multimodal agents because visible correctness is part of the task, and direct visual feedback improves results on that harder setting.
